comment: Step 8 - react-router 7, the effects that are not effects, and two budgets.
The line's entry for this step is "Router 7 (framework mode) or server
components for read-heavy routes, react-hooks v6 rules, bundle budgets".
Framework mode and server components are both ruled out by properties of this
application rather than by preference: it routes on the hash, which framework
mode does not do, and the scorer serves the candidate's dist/ from a static
mock server, so there is no node process for a server component to render in.
What is left of the line is the router major, the two rules the step before
this one deliberately did not read, and the budgets.
Measured before the spec was written (NOTES-authoring.md, "Step 8's
groundwork"): the arriving tree reaches the router through 44
react-router-dom import statements across 44 files, with twelve distinct
names, and all twelve are exported by react-router 7's own root entry, so the
move is a rename.  react-hooks/exhaustive-deps and
react-hooks/set-state-in-effect - the two rules step 7's spec left out
because they are this step's subject - report 85 findings between them.  178
useState calls arrive; the reference solution leaves 24.
The budgets are where the measuring mattered.  The entry wall does not move:
140000 bytes, the figure three steps have already used.  What changes is that
it becomes work.  react-router 7's client router is larger than the 6 it
replaces - 9602 gzipped bytes in this tree's entry chunk, 134332 before and
143934 after, against 5668 of room - so the step that installs it goes over a
wall it inherited comfortably, and something has to leave the entry.  The
reference solution takes the first page's carousel out and lands at 138485.
The second budget measures a chart screen rather than the no-such-route
screen the first one measures, because a split entry is easiest to make look
good on a screen that draws nothing: 286131 bytes across fifteen chunks to
put the visitor-count chart at #/statistics/total on the page.
27 of the 54 gate points are the step's own work and are read on any tree.
27 are the twenty-four invariants the seven steps behind this one built, and
they are credited only once this step's key is met: the router installed at
7, and the two effect rules down to a quarter of what arrived.

checks.why: The router this project runs on is react-router, at version 7. Read out of the installed tree rather than out of package.json, because a range in a manifest is a request and what routes the application is what npm actually put in node_modules - and because a single copy is half of what is being asked: two majors installed at once means something still depends on the old one, which is exactly the state a rename that left react-router-dom behind produces. Version 7 and not whatever is newest: react-router's latest is 8.4.0 at the time this step was written, so `npm install react-router` lands on 8 and this check has live teeth rather than being satisfied by accident. The instruction states the version, so a tree that arrives on 8 is a candidate that did not read it rather than a requirement nobody stated.

And react-router-dom is not a dependency any more. Since version 7 the published react-router-dom is a re-export shim - 7.18.4 has one dependency, react-router 7.18.4, and no code of its own - so a tree that renamed its imports and left the package installed is a tree that still ships a package it does not use and still pins a second version of the router that can drift from the first. Two rather than one because this is the half of the rename that gets forgotten: the imports are what the compiler complains about and the manifest is not.

No module imports from react-router-dom. The tree arrives with forty-four such statements across forty-four files - one each - and every name in them is exported by react-router itself, so this is a rename and not a rewrite: checked against the published package rather than assumed, all twelve distinct names the tree imports are on react-router 7's root entry. Graded against the forty-four so that a candidate who misses one file loses a fraction of this check rather than the check, and counted by the same scan that reads every other import in this repository. The package is counted by any spelling that reaches it - the bare name, a path into its build output, or a require of either - so a tree that keeps the shim installed and imports it past its own entry reads its imports here rather than reading zero.

The effects that are not effects are gone. These are the two rules the step before this one deliberately left out of its fifteen - the one about dependency arrays and the one about setting state from an effect - and they are left out there because they are the subject here. The tree arrives with eighty-five findings between them, which is what derived state written as an effect looks like from the outside: a value computed into state by an effect that watches the value it was computed from, one render late and one dependency array away from a loop. Graded against the eighty-five, because this is the largest single piece of work in the step and a candidate who clears eighty of them has done the step. Suppressions count as findings, the way they do everywhere else in this suite: commenting the rule out moves the count sideways rather than down, and the rule that is switched off is the rule this check exists to enforce. One guard, and it is about the first of the two rules rather than about the step: the dependency rule has nothing to ask of an effect that has no dependency list, because no list means after every render, which is never wrong about its dependencies. So a tree can empty this count out by deleting forty-four lists instead of by answering them, and the guard is the ceiling on how many effects may end up running on every render. Three arrive that way and the reference solution leaves two - the effects whose whole body is keeping a ref pointed at the latest prop are not counted at all, because running after every render is that idiom's entire purpose and React's own guidance writes it with no list. Twelve is four times what arrives: room for a tree that made a different but honest choice about an effect or two, and nowhere near the number of lists there are to delete.

guard.unmet: more than twelve of this tree's effects run after every render because they carry no dependency list at all, and an effect with no list is never asked about its dependencies - so the finding count beside this one is low partly because the question stopped being put. The one kind of effect that is right to have no list is the one whose whole body keeps a ref pointed at the latest value, and those are not counted here; twelve is six times what the reference solution has left

checks.why: And the second subject the line asks for: what a visitor waits for when they arrive cold at a chart screen, under 296000 bytes gzipped. The address is the visitor-count chart under the statistics layout, and the wait ends when the chart library has taken that container over, which is the attribute echarts stamps on the element as it initialises. The container being in the document is not that instant and is far too early - the empty div renders before the panel's own chunk has arrived. Initialisation is not literally the first painted pixel either: echarts 3.8.5 sets the attribute inside init(), a few statements before setOption draws. For a byte count the two are the same cut, because nothing is fetched between them - every module the draw needs is already resolved for init() to have been called at all - and initialisation is the later of the two instants that can be observed from outside without reading the library's internals. Measured with the same instrument as the entry wall, off the same production build, at a second address - so it costs a page load rather than a build, and the stage's own 120 s cap is not shared with anything below it. This address and not the largest chunk in the tree: both modules on the way to it are awaited by the router as part of the navigation rather than suspended behind a fallback, so nothing paints until all of the javascript has arrived and the number is the whole of what the visitor waits for - and it is a number both halves of this step move, down when the route stays split and the effects stop pulling work forward, back up if the split is undone. Measured: the reference solution fetches 286131 bytes gzipped across fifteen chunks to put that chart on the screen - the entry, the statistics layout, the calendar, the tools module, the panel itself, and ten of echarts' own pieces, of which the line chart is 90632 on its own. The wall is that number with 9869 of room, about three and a half per cent, and the room is deliberate: unlike the entry, this figure barely moves when a tree splits differently, because bytes moved out of the entry into a chunk this screen needs are bytes this screen still fetches. What it refuses is a tree that made the screen genuinely heavier - one that lost the echarts split, or that pulled the whole chart library in where the tree had been importing its pieces, or that duplicated a shared module into several chunks while chasing the entry wall. And a tree that simply failed the entry wall is not charged for it twice: leave the entry at 143934 and this screen costs about 291580, which passes here and fails there, which is the division of labour between the two.

checks.why: And the development console is still silent under StrictMode's double invocation, at the count the two steps before this one set. It keeps its four points rather than dropping to an inherited one because this is the reading §2 is most likely to move, and the instruction says so: an effect that computed a value into state and a render that computes the same value are not equally forgiving about a store that has not answered yet. The effect ran after a render that had already guarded itself; the render has to guard itself. Read undefined off a slice the store has not filled and this is where it is heard, in a build made with NODE_ENV=development and driven across one address per layout, every compare-by-seller screen, and an address no route matches. Four guards stand in front of it besides the usual chain, and they are the whole reason a count can be trusted: the development build has to actually be a development build, StrictMode has to be on around every root, no module may reassign or wrap console, and the build may not be configured to drop the calls before they run. A count of zero taken from a tree that removed the reporting is a count of nothing.

checks.why: The compiler ran on the javascript the site serves. Read out of the build rather than out of the configuration that asks for it: a compiled function allocates a memo cache and initialises each slot by comparing it against Symbol.for("react.memo_cache_sentinel"), which is the runtime contract between the compiler's output and react/compiler-runtime, and what is read is that cache-slot comparison, once for every slot the compiler allocated. The comparison is a construct rather than a name: it survives minification, because the symbol is the argument to Symbol.for and renaming the identifiers around it leaves the shape intact. That makes this a reading of the artifact and not of the intention, and it is indifferent to which route enabled the compiler. Counting the name on its own would not do, in either direction: React's own DOM package names the same symbol where it defines it, and a definition is an assignment rather than a slot being initialised, while a chunk that merely spells the string out - once, or a hundred times over in one literal - is not compiled output and is not paid as though it were. Measured over the chunks the built page reaches, so a compiled chunk nothing loads is not credited: the arriving tree reports none, a tree with the compiler switched on and its source untouched reports 326, and the reference solution reports 444.
